H₂ particles are one-fourth as fast as O₂ particles.
H₂ and O₂ particles have the same average speed.

Assume both solutions are measured at the same wavelength in the same cell and remain in the linear Beer-Lambert range.
A sample of gas has a volume of 5.0 L at a pressure of 1.0 atm. It is compressed to 2.0 L at constant temperature with no gas added or removed. The final pressure of the gas is

A rigid flask contains nitrogen gas that behaves nearly ideally at 300 K. When the flask is cooled to 80 K, near the boiling point of N2, the measured pressure is lower than the ideal gas law predicts. Which statement best explains why?

choices.choice_text: At 80 K the molecules stop moving entirely, so the pressure falls to nearly zero regardless of what the ideal gas law predicts.
At 80 K the slower N2 molecules attract one another noticeably, so they strike the walls less forcefully than ideal particles would.
At 80 K the N2 molecules become polar and develop permanent dipoles, so strong dipole-dipole forces act between them.
At 80 K the volume of the N2 molecules is no longer negligible, so the available volume is smaller and the pressure drops below ideal.

stem: Surface ocean water near the poles (about 2 °C) contains more dissolved CO₂(g) than surface water near the equator (about 28 °C), even though the air above both regions has the same pressure and the same composition. Which statement best explains this difference?

choices.choice_text: At low temperature, CO₂ molecules become more polar, so they are attracted more strongly to the polar water molecules around them.
Colder water forms stronger ion-dipole attractions with CO₂ molecules, and these attractions hold the CO₂ in solution.
Colder water is denser, and the extra weight of the water above pushes more CO₂ gas down into the solution.
In the colder water, CO₂ molecules have lower average kinetic energy, so fewer of them overcome their weak attractions to water and escape, and more CO₂ stays dissolved.

stem: A 2.50 x 10^-5 M solution of an organic dye has an absorbance of 0.600 at its wavelength of maximum absorbance, where its molar absorptivity is 1.20 x 10^4 M^-1 cm^-1. What is the path length of the cuvette used?

Photon P has a wavelength of 5.0 x 10^-7 m. Photon Q has a frequency of 4.0 x 10^14 s^-1. (Take the speed of light as 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.) Which statement correctly compares the energies of the two photons?

choices.choice_text: The two photons have equal energy, because both travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum regardless of wavelength or frequency.
Photon Q has more energy, because its given value of 4.0 x 10^14 is numerically far larger than the 5.0 x 10^-7 given for photon P.
Photon Q has about 1.5 times the energy of photon P, because λ = c/ν = 7.5 x 10^-7 m for Q, which is longer than 5.0 x 10^-7 m for P.
Photon P has about 1.5 times the energy of photon Q, because ν = c/λ = 6.0 x 10^14 s^-1 for P, which is greater than 4.0 x 10^14 s^-1 for Q.

stem: A student pours a clear blue solution of CuSO₄(aq) through filter paper into a clean flask, hoping to collect the CuSO₄ on the paper. The filtrate in the flask is still blue and the paper holds back nothing. Which statement best explains this result?

choices.choice_text: The dissolved Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions are individually dispersed among water molecules and are far smaller than the pores in the paper, so they pass through with the water.
Filtration separates liquids from other liquids according to density, so it cannot affect a solute that is dissolved in the liquid.
The pores in the filter paper were too large for this solute, and a finer-pore filter would have trapped the Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions on the paper.
Filtration separates substances by polarity, and the polar water and the ionic CuSO₄ both pass through the polar filter paper together.

stem: A student adds 85.0 mL of distilled water to 15.0 mL of 0.800 M KMnO₄(aq) and mixes thoroughly, assuming the volumes are additive. What is the molarity of the resulting solution?

The electronegativities of hydrogen and chlorine are given below.

Atom | Electronegativity
H | 2.2
Cl | 3.2

Which statement best describes the H–Cl bond and explains how its bonding electrons are distributed?

choices.choice_text: The bond is polar covalent because Cl attracts the shared electrons more strongly than H, giving Cl a partial negative charge.
The bond is nonpolar covalent because both atoms are nonmetals and therefore share the bonding electrons equally.
The bond is polar covalent because H attracts the shared electrons more strongly than Cl, giving H a partial negative charge.
The bond is ionic because any difference in electronegativity means an electron is completely transferred between the atoms.

stem:
Methanol, CH₃OH, contains a single bond between a carbon atom and an oxygen atom. The electronegativity values are shown in the table below.

Atom | Electronegativity
C | 2.6
O | 3.4

Which claim about the C–O bond in methanol, including its justification, is best supported by these data?

choices.choice_text: The C–O bond is nonpolar covalent because carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share the bonding electrons equally.
The C–O bond is polar covalent because C pulls the shared electron pair more strongly than O does, so C carries a partial negative charge.
The C–O bond is polar covalent because O pulls the shared electron pair more strongly than C does, so O carries a partial negative charge.
The C–O bond is ionic because any difference in electronegativity means an electron is completely transferred from C to O.

stem: A student is given potential energy (PE) data for two hydrogen atoms as a function of internuclear distance. PE is defined as 0 kJ/mol for fully separated atoms. Data (distance in pm, PE in kJ/mol): 40, +250; 60, −380; 74, −436; 100, −360; 150, −150; 300, −5. The student plots internuclear distance on the x-axis. Which description of the correctly drawn graph is accurate?

choices.choice_text: With x in pm and y in kJ/mol, the curve rises steeply below about 50 pm, reaches a minimum at (74 pm, −436 kJ/mol), and levels off toward 0 kJ/mol at large distances.
With x in pm and y in kJ/mol, the curve reaches a minimum at 74 pm and then levels off at −436 kJ/mol at large distances.
With x in pm and y in kJ/mol, the bond length is shown where the curve crosses 0 kJ/mol, near 50 pm, and the minimum marks where the atoms separate.
With x in pm and y in kJ/mol, the curve rises to a maximum of +436 kJ/mol at 74 pm, because energy must be added to break the bond.

stem: A chemistry student models the bond in a Cl₂ molecule using calculated potential energy values for two chlorine atoms at several internuclear distances. The potential energy of two completely separated Cl atoms is set at 0 kJ/mol. Data (internuclear distance in pm, potential energy in kJ/mol): 150, +300; 180, −150; 199, −242; 230, −200; 300, −80; 500, −3. The student will put internuclear distance on the horizontal axis. Which statement correctly describes the graph the student should draw?

choices.choice_text: With distance in pm and energy in kJ/mol, the curve bottoms out at 199 pm and then flattens at −242 kJ/mol as the distance keeps increasing.
With distance in pm and energy in kJ/mol, the curve climbs steeply at distances below about 180 pm, bottoms out at (199 pm, −242 kJ/mol), and flattens toward 0 kJ/mol at large distances.
With distance in pm and energy in kJ/mol, the bond length is shown where the curve crosses 0 kJ/mol, near 170 pm, and the lowest point marks where the atoms separate.
With distance in pm and energy in kJ/mol, the curve rises to a peak of +242 kJ/mol at 199 pm, because energy must be added to break the bond.

stem: A student is constructing a potential-energy-versus-internuclear-distance model comparing a C–C single bond with a C=C double bond. Both curves use zero potential energy for fully separated atoms. How should the student represent the double-bond curve relative to the single-bond curve?

choices.choice_text: Place its minimum at a smaller internuclear distance and a more negative potential energy.
Place its minimum at a greater internuclear distance and a more negative potential energy.
Place its minimum at a smaller internuclear distance and a less negative potential energy.
Place its minimum at the same internuclear distance and a more negative potential energy.

stem: For a lab report, a student sketches two potential-energy-versus-internuclear-distance curves on one set of axes: one for the N–N single bond in hydrazine and one for the N≡N triple bond in nitrogen gas. Potential energy is set to zero for fully separated atoms. How should the student draw the triple-bond curve compared with the single-bond curve?

choices.choice_text: Its minimum should sit at a shorter internuclear distance and lie farther below zero.
Its minimum should sit at a longer internuclear distance and lie farther below zero.
Its minimum should sit at a shorter internuclear distance and lie closer to zero.
Its minimum should sit at the same internuclear distance and lie farther below zero.

stem: When struck, a crystal of an ionic compound fractures rather than bending. Which explanation best connects this behavior to the arrangement of particles in the solid?

choices.choice_text: The crystal consists of separate neutral molecules whose weak attractions allow them to pull apart when struck.
Displacement of a layer can bring like-charged ions next to one another, and their repulsion causes the crystal to fracture.
Layers of ions slide freely while maintaining their attractive interactions, allowing the crystal to fracture.
Displacement of a layer brings like-charged ions together, and their attraction pulls the crystal apart.

stem: A student taps a small chisel against a crystal of potassium bromide, KBr. Instead of flattening or denting, the crystal shatters into smaller pieces with flat faces. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for this observation?

choices.choice_text: Solid KBr is made of individual neutral KBr molecules held together by weak forces, so the molecules separate easily when the crystal is struck.
The blow shifts one plane of ions relative to the next so that K⁺ ions sit beside K⁺ ions and Br⁻ beside Br⁻, and the resulting repulsion splits the crystal.
Planes of K⁺ and Br⁻ ions glide past one another while each ion keeps oppositely charged neighbors, so the crystal breaks apart.
Shifting a plane of ions places like-charged ions side by side, and the attraction between those like charges pulls the crystal apart.

stem: A pure ionic compound has a high melting temperature. Which particle-level model best explains this observation?

choices.choice_text: The solid consists of separate cation–anion pairs; melting requires breaking the strong attraction within every pair.
Cations and anions form a repeating array; the high melting temperature results mainly from the large masses of the ions.
Cations and anions form an extended, repeating array; melting requires substantial energy to disrupt many strong attractions throughout the array.
The solid contains neutral atoms formed when cations and anions lose their charges; strong attractions between these atoms explain its high melting temperature.

stem: Magnesium oxide, MgO, is used to line furnaces because it can remain solid while metals inside the furnace are molten. Which particle-level explanation best accounts for the lining’s resistance to melting?

choices.choice_text: MgO consists of individual Mg²⁺–O²⁻ pairs, and the strong attraction inside each independent pair makes the lining difficult to melt.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions occupy a repeating lattice, but their large particle masses are the main reason the lining resists melting.
The positive and negative charges cancel within MgO, leaving neutral atoms whose strong mutual attractions prevent the lining from melting.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions occupy a repeating three-dimensional lattice whose numerous strong electrostatic attractions require considerable energy to disrupt.

stem: A solid alloy contains metals X and Y. Their atomic radii are X: 128 pm and Y: 135 pm. The alloy conducts electricity. Which particulate-level model best explains both the alloy’s structure and its electrical conductivity?

choices.choice_text: Y atoms occupy gaps between X atoms, and mobile, delocalized valence electrons carry current throughout the solid.
Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and positive metal ions move through the solid to carry current.
Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and valence electrons confined to individual metal atoms carry current throughout the solid.
Y atoms replace some X atoms at lattice positions, and mobile, delocalized valence electrons carry current throughout the solid.

stem: A steel wire carries current in an electrical circuit. The steel consists mainly of iron with a small amount of carbon added. For this model, the atomic radii are 126 pm for iron and 77 pm for carbon. Which description connects the wire’s alloy structure with its ability to conduct electricity?

choices.choice_text: Carbon atoms substitute for iron atoms at lattice sites; delocalized valence electrons move through the wire and transport charge.
Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; positive iron ions travel through the wire and transport charge.
Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; delocalized valence electrons move through the wire and transport charge.
Carbon atoms fit into spaces within the iron framework; valence electrons remain attached to individual iron atoms while transporting charge through the wire.

stem: A sample of a pure metal is hammered into a thinner sheet without breaking. Which particulate-level model best explains this observation?

choices.choice_text: Layers of positive metal ions slide past one another while the mobile, delocalized valence electrons continue to hold the solid together.
Layers of alternating positive and negative ions slide past one another while attractions between oppositely charged ions hold the solid together.
The positive metal ions remain in their original positions while the surrounding electron sea becomes thinner and wider.
Layers of metal atoms slide past one another because each atom’s valence electrons remain localized on that atom.

stem: A straight wire made of pure copper is bent into a loop without cracking. Which particulate-level description best accounts for the wire’s ability to change shape while remaining intact?

choices.choice_text: Positive and negative copper ions shift relative to one another, while attractions between these oppositely charged ions keep the wire intact.
Positive copper ions stay at their original locations, while only the surrounding electron sea curves into the wire’s new shape.
Copper atoms shift relative to one another, while valence electrons confined to their individual atoms keep the wire intact.
Positive copper ions shift relative to one another, while mobile valence electrons distributed throughout the solid maintain attractions that hold it together.

stem: Which description represents a complete, correct Lewis diagram for OH⁻? In every description, the entire structure is enclosed in brackets with a − charge written outside. Each lone pair contains two electrons.

choices.choice_text: One O–H single bond, three lone pairs on O, and no lone pairs on H.
One O–H single bond, two lone pairs on O, and no lone pairs on H.
One O–H single bond and no lone pairs on either atom.
One O=H double bond, two lone pairs on O, and no lone pairs on H.
